title: Prologue (lines 1–98)

teacherSummary.text: Before dawn after the war, Antigone tells her sister Ismene that King Creon has forbidden anyone to bury their brother Polyneices, who attacked Thebes; Eteocles, who defended it, will be buried with honour. Antigone will bury Polyneices and asks Ismene to help. Ismene, recalling the ruin of their family, refuses: they are women and cannot defy the State. Antigone goes alone.

context.history: For Greeks, leaving a body unburied denied the dead rest and offended the gods. The two brothers had killed each other in the war over Thebes; this play was written before Oedipus Rex and Oedipus at Colonus, though its story comes last.

significance: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges.
discussionQuestions: When, if ever, is it right to break a law?
Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with divine law and human law?

satQuestions.passage:
Ismene, sister of my blood and heart,
See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfil
The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes!
For what of pain, affliction, outrage, shame,
Is lacking in our fortunes, thine and mine?
And now this proclamation of today
Made by our Captain-General to the State,
What can its purport be? Didst hear and heed,
Or art thou deaf when friends are banned as foes?
To me, Antigone, no word of friends
Has come, or glad or grievous, since we twain
Were reft of our two brethren in one day
By double fratricide; and since i’ the night
Our Argive leaguers fled, no later news
Has reached me, to inspirit or deject.

anchorPassages.note: The edict that drives the play: one brother buried, the other denied rites on pain of stoning.
anchorPassages.text:
What but the thought of our two brothers dead,
The one by Creon graced with funeral rites,
The other disappointed? Eteocles
He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports)
With obsequies that use and wont ordain,
So gracing him among the dead below.
But Polyneices, a dishonoured corse,
(So by report the royal edict runs)
No man may bury him or make lament—
Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast
For kites to scent afar and swoop upon.
Such is the edict (if report speak true)
Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed
At thee and me, aye me too; and anon
He will be here to promulgate, for such
As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth
No passing humour, for the edict says
Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death.

anchorPassages.note: Ismene's prudence as foil: obedience to the State over risky piety. Resumes after skipped method line 53.
anchorPassages.text:
And last, our hapless brethren in one day,
Both in a mutual destiny involved,
Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain.
Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone;
Shall we not perish wretchedest of all.
If in defiance of the law we cross
A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that,
Not framed by nature to contend with men.
Remember this too that the stronger rules;
We must obey his orders, these or worse.
Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat
The dead to pardon. I perforce obey
The powers that be. ’Tis foolishness, I ween,
To overstep in aught the golden mean.

anchorPassages.text:
I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still,
I would not welcome such a fellowship.
Go thine own way; myself will bury him.
How sweet to die in such employ, to rest—
Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace—
A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth,
But by the dead commended; and with them
I shall abide for ever. As for thee,
Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
I scorn them not, but to defy the State
Or break her ordinance I have no skill.
A specious pretext. I will go alone
To lap my dearest brother in the grave.

weDoAnswers: For Greeks, leaving a body unburied denied the dead rest and offended the gods. The two brothers had killed each other in the war over Thebes; this play was written before Oedipus Rex and Oedipus at Colonus, though its story comes last. Read closely: “But Polyneices, a dishonoured corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon.” (Antigone, lines 25–29).
analysis.weDoWords: “Dishonoured”, “tombless” and “unwept” stand out in lines 25–29. Each word names a rite the edict denies Polyneices—honour, a grave, and lament—so Antigone shows how harsh Creon’s order is before she says what she will do about it. “Dishonoured corse” already judges the decree in a single phrase.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Ismene, sister of my blood and heart, / See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfil / The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes” slowly and put it in my own words: Antigone opens by naming Ismene as her blood sister and by claiming that Zeus is completing Oedipus’s inherited doom in their own lives. Next, craft. “Sister of my blood and heart” binds the two women before any dispute, and “the weird of Oedipus, a world of woes” piles the family curse into one phrase so the new trouble already feels inherited. The strongest word is “Oedipus”: it packs the inherited doom into one name before any choice is spoken. Then, effect. What do lines 1–3 reveal about two sisters, one choice? My answer: The sisters will embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene’s “weak women” (line 60) states her society’s view of women, which Antigone’s action challenges. The opening already sets the family past as the pressure under which that choice is made.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. Useful evidence: “Ismene, sister of my blood and heart, / See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfil / The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes” (Prologue, lines 1–3): Antigone, lines 1–3. Theme link: The edict denies Polyneices the rites the gods require (no burial, no lament), so a human order collides with divine custom before Antigone acts. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: Which character in “Prologue (lines 1–98)” acts most wisely in the matter of two sisters, one choice, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.

What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. Useful evidence: “But Polyneices, a dishonoured corse, / (So by report the royal edict runs) / No man may bury him or make lament— / Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast / For kites to scent afar and swoop upon” (Prologue, lines 25–29): Antigone, lines 25–29. On characterization: Antigone speaks in commands and tests (“If thou art worthy of thy blood or base”); Ismene answers with memory and fear, so their speech styles already carry the choice. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
